source: Hofstadter lecture test of Cope EMI (via Wikipedia article)
finding: Hofstadter played a genuine Chopin piece and an EMI Chopin-style piece to audiences. They did no better than chance at telling which was which.
numbers: Chance-level identification; no counts given.
limits: No counts or percentages in the article. Informal lecture audiences, not a controlled study. Cope deleted the EMI database in 2005.
agent_relevance: Imitation tests are weak evidence of creativity. Do not use 'fooled listeners' as a quality signal.

source: Wikipedia: Experiments in Musical Intelligence
finding: EMI began in 1981 to help Cope's composer's block. By 2001 it was about 20,000 lines of Lisp. It was applied to Bach, Mozart, Chopin, Bartok, Brahms and others.
numbers: About 20,000 lines of Lisp (2001); started 1981.
limits: No independent replication or Turing-style study is described in the article. Output is recombination of a human corpus in a known style.
agent_relevance: Recombination of a corpus can look creative. Check where novelty comes from.

source: Wikipedia: AARON (Harold Cohen)
finding: AARON could not learn new styles or imagery on its own. Cohen added each capability by hand from 1972 to 2016, and would not call it creative.
numbers: Development 1972 to 2016; C then Lisp in early 1990s.
limits: Source code never released. Claim that output follows a recognisable formula is tagged as needing a citation.
agent_relevance: A scaffold with fixed rules has a ceiling set by its author.

source: Binsted, Pain and Ritchie (1997) children's judgments of JAPE riddles (via secondary summary)
finding: Children aged 8 to 11 rated JAPE riddles, human riddles, and non-jokes for jokiness, funniness and familiarity. JAPE riddles were seen as jokes. They were rated less funny on average than human riddles, but some were as funny.
numbers: 8 to 11 year olds; no numbers on the page I opened.
limits: Only a secondary summary was opened; original is Pragmatics and Cognition 5(2). Other sources say no significant difference for the most comprehensible JAPE texts, so sources conflict on funniness.
agent_relevance: Separate 'reads as a joke' from 'is funny'. Measure both.

source: Hessel et al. (2023) Do Androids Laugh at Electric Sheep? New Yorker caption benchmarks
finding: Best multimodal model scored 62 percent on 5-way caption matching from pixels. Humans scored 94 percent. With ground-truth scene descriptions GPT-4 (5-shot) reached 84.5 percent.
numbers: 62 vs 94 percent (pixels); GPT-4 5-shot 84.5 percent (descriptions).
limits: Human-authored explanations beat the best machine ones (few-shot GPT-4) in over 2/3 of head-to-head cases. FT-GPT-3 lost to humans in 87.8 percent of earlier pairs.
agent_relevance: Humor understanding depends on perception; give the agent a good description of the input first.

source: Hessel et al. (2023) explanation and quality-ranking results
finding: Fine-tuned GPT-3 predicted New Yorker editor picks better than three humans but did worse at predicting crowd votes. Image information raised explanation quality.
numbers: NYAcc GPT-3 69.8 vs human estimate 64.6. Image T5-11B beat caption-only in 84.7 percent; T5-11B beat T5-Large in 68.5 percent.
limits: Model without image information lost in 74.6 percent. Still below humans.
agent_relevance: Models can predict the taste of an editor group; that is not the same as being funny.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Humor in AI: cartoon captioning preferences
finding: Dataset of over 250 million ratings on over 2.2 million captions across 365 contests. GPT-4 and Claude underperform top human contestants. RLHF and DPO gave limited gains. Best-of-N on a reward model beat PPO.
numbers: Claude 3 Opus captions preferred over human top-10 captions only 34 percent of the time by crowd raters. 91 of 358 contests held out.
limits: Win rates on 91 held-out cartoons. Crowd raters from Prolific plus one expert.
agent_relevance: For creative output, sample many and filter with a good judge.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) evaluator reliability for humor
finding: Judge accuracy for telling rank 1-10 captions from rank 1000-1009 captions was about 61 to 67 percent in pairwise mode. Group comparison was more accurate. A former New Yorker cartoon editor outperformed all other evaluators.
numbers: Pairwise: crowd workers about 61 percent, GPT-4-Turbo text description 67 percent (200 pairs, error about 3.4 points).
limits: LLM judges beat average crowd workers but not the expert.
agent_relevance: LLM judges of humor are only moderately reliable. Compare in groups, not pairs.

source: Jentzsch and Kersting (2023) ChatGPT is fun, but it is not funny
finding: Over 90 percent of 1008 ChatGPT jokes were the same 25 jokes. The top four made up over 50 percent.
numbers: 1008 samples; 25 distinct top jokes cover over 90 percent.
limits: Prompts in fresh chats. Some jokes were modified, so not hard-coded. Authors guess RLHF memorisation but could not test it. One model, June 2023.
agent_relevance: Repeated outputs mean low diversity. Use varied sampling and dedupe.

source: Jentzsch and Kersting (2023) joke explanation and detection
finding: ChatGPT explained valid jokes well but invented explanations for invalid jokes. Joke-typical features could mislead it in joke detection.
numbers: Exploratory; no formal effect sizes.
limits: Exploratory, one model, one version.
agent_relevance: Form cues can fool classifiers; test with form-matched negatives.

source: Gomez-Rodriguez and Williams (2023) A Confederacy of Models
finding: Twelve LLMs and 5 human creative-writing students wrote a combat story. GPT-4 scored 80.2 overall. Best open model (Koala) scored 60.0. Humans led on originality.
numbers: GPT-4 80.2 vs Koala 60.0. Weighted kappa 0.48 (CI 0.43 to 0.54). Overall-score Pearson 0.58.
limits: Two raters per story, volunteers, 10 ratings per model. No significant human vs top-6 LLM difference on overall score (low power). Per-item pooled (N 100): GPT-4 better than humans, p = 0.00031.
agent_relevance: Fluency is largely solved. Originality is the open gap.

source: Gomez-Rodriguez and Williams (2023) humor result
finding: Humor was the hardest rubric item. A binary split: Claude, Bing, GPT-4 and humans scored in the upper group. The rest failed.
numbers: Mean humor 3.4 across models; best 6.5.
limits: Single prompt, small sample, subjective item.
agent_relevance: Test humor on a few probes before relying on a model.

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) Art or Artifice? Torrance Test of Creative Writing
finding: 48 stories judged by 10 expert writers on 14 binary tests. New Yorker stories passed 84.7 percent (11.9 of 14). GPT-3.5 under 10 percent. GPT-4 and Claude 1.3 about 30 percent. LLM stories pass 3 to 10 times fewer tests.
numbers: 12 human, 36 LLM stories; about 1400 words; 3 ratings per story. Fleiss kappa 0.41 average; aggregate Pearson 0.69.
limits: Moderate per-test agreement. GPT-4 was best on originality. Models from 2023.
agent_relevance: Product-level tests show a large gap to professionals.

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) LLMs as creativity judges
finding: Three LLMs used as TTCW judges correlated with experts close to zero. GPT-4 got above 0.2 on only two of 14 tests. Few-shot prompts for a couple of tests did not help.
numbers: Correlations near 0 across 48 stories.
limits: Mostly zero-shot prompts. Contrasts with work finding GPT-4 acceptable on short responses under 100 words.
agent_relevance: Do not use an LLM self-judge to rank long creative drafts without calibration.

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) authorship attribution
finding: Experts attributed New Yorker stories mostly to experienced writers. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 stories were attributed to AI over 80 percent of the time. Claude 1.3 stories were more often called amateur than AI.
numbers: Over 80 percent AI attribution for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
limits: Authors guess familiarity with OpenAI styles; not tested.
agent_relevance: Stylistic tells exist and readers learn them.

source: Padmakumar and He (2024) Does Writing with Language Models Reduce Content Diversity?
finding: In 300 essays (10 per topic per condition, 10 topics), corpus homogenization was higher with InstructGPT than solo or GPT-3 (p < 0.05). GPT-3 co-writing did not change it significantly.
numbers: Rouge-L key-point homogenization: Solo 0.1536, GPT-3 0.1578, InstructGPT 0.1660.
limits: Upwork writers, argumentative essays not fiction. Users queried the model about 9 times and kept about 70 percent of suggestions.
agent_relevance: RLHF-style tuning lowers the diversity of what a tool offers. Keep a diverse base proposer.

source: Padmakumar and He (2024) diversity measures
finding: InstructGPT co-written essays had the lowest unique n-gram fraction and fewest unique key points at every clustering threshold, and repeated more 5-grams. User-written text was unaffected; model-contributed key points were more alike.
numbers: Lowest n-gram and key-point diversity for InstructGPT at all thresholds.
limits: Decoding was set to high randomness (temperature 0.9, frequency penalty 0.5), and still less diverse.
agent_relevance: Temperature does not repair tuning-driven mode collapse.

source: Xu et al. (2025) Echoes in AI: Sui Generis score
finding: LLM stories reuse plot elements across generations. GPT-4 and LLaMA-3 segments scored significantly lower Sui Generis scores than human segments on both datasets.
numbers: 100 stories (50 WritingPrompts, 50 Wikipedia plot summaries); K = 20 continuations; std 1.1 across instruction prompts.
limits: Cross-model scores slightly higher but close. Peer-reviewed in PNAS 2025.
agent_relevance: Same plot ideas come back across samples. Measure plot-level repetition, not just wording.

source: Xu et al. (2025) validation of the Sui Generis score
finding: Score correlated 0.55 with human surprise ratings. Homogenization score and embedding similarity correlated only about 0.46 and 0.50 with human judgment. Paraphrase moved Sui Generis 4 percent but perplexity 15 percent.
numbers: Spearman about 0.55 (SG), 0.46 and 0.50 (others).
limits: Segment-level human grading; small human study.
agent_relevance: Use entailment-style checks for novelty of ideas, not n-gram overlap.

source: Tian et al. (2024) Are LLMs capable of generating human-level narratives?
finding: LLM stories are homogeneously positive and lack tension. Riches to Rags and Oedipus arcs are 14.6 and 9.3 percent of human stories but 1.3 and 1.7 percent of GPT-4 stories.
numbers: Human 14.6 and 9.3 percent vs GPT-4 1.3 and 1.7 percent; Rags to Riches 4.4 percent human.
limits: Expert plus automatic annotation. Models also weak at identifying story arcs (GPT-3.5 near 0.2 exact agreement against 1/7 chance).
agent_relevance: Add explicit arc and turning-point planning before drafting.

source: Tian et al. (2024) discourse-aware generation
finding: Putting story arc or turning points into prompts raised diversity, suspense and arousal, by over 40 percent on the paper's measures.
numbers: Over 40 percent improvement reported in the abstract.
limits: Gains are on suspense, arousal and diversity, not general quality. Structure was model-generated.
agent_relevance: A plan step with arc and turning points is a cheap scaffold.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) Leap-of-Thought (CLoT) for Oogiri humor
finding: Oogiri-GO has over 130,000 samples in English, Chinese and Japanese. On Qwen-VL, instruction tuning raised accuracy by 6.8, 6.7 and 4.3 points over three task types. Full CLoT raised it by 9.1, 10.4 and 8.2 points.
numbers: 130,000 samples; 77.95 percent with like counts; gains 4.3 to 10.4 points.
limits: Choice and ranking tasks, not funniness of free output. English IT2T unavailable due to cultural preference.
agent_relevance: Associative generation plus self-refinement (rank, keep top-2, mix with ground truth) is a candidate pattern.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) failure of existing LLMs and CoT on Oogiri
finding: Most existing LLMs, including GPT-4v, did poorly in the Oogiri game. Chain-of-thought style prompts did not fix this.
numbers: No single figure recorded.
limits: Authors also say plain fine-tuning on the data did not help much.
agent_relevance: CoT is not enough for humor. A funniness judge step is a weak link.

source: Humor reasoning-path training (ICLR 2025, structured thought leaps)
finding: Training on multi-hop reasoning paths raised average English accuracy over LLaMA3-70B and GPT-4o.
numbers: Gains of 4.55 and 5.91 points against LLaMA3-70B and GPT-4o.
limits: Human preference study on 200 text questions; three experts rated logical coherence on 200 examples. Tencent QQ work.
agent_relevance: Reasoning traces help humor judgement; effect is a few points.

source: Wordcraft: a Human-AI Collaborative Editor for Story Writing (2021)
finding: Wordcraft is an AI editor for story planning, writing and editing. Early users said it helped from rephrasing to continuing text.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Extended abstract. No formal user study. Authors planned a systematic study.
agent_relevance: Human-in-loop tools were first judged by anecdote.
